rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The likeness either confirms the warning that the Hour will arrive swiftly, or answers mockers who impatiently ask when it will come: after the warning they will have waited only briefly.
rows.anchor: إما تقرير وتأكيد لما ينبيء عنه الإنذار من سرعة مجيء المنذر به

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: The compact wording replaces “only an hour of the day, its evening or forenoon”; possessive suffixes rule out imagining an interval from one day's evening until another day's forenoon.
rows.anchor: على ما نقل عن الزمخشري له أصل وهو لم يلبثوا إلا ساعة من نهار عشيته أو ضحاه

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Tibi allows evening or forenoon to stand metaphorically for the whole day; adding the pronoun reinforces this and excludes the broader possibility, like saying one saw something with one's own eyes.
rows.anchor: وقال الطيبي إنه من المحتمل أن يراد بالعشية أو الضحى كل اليوم مجازا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi prefers the less forced explanation of the added pronoun, while allowing it to reinforce the whole-day interpretation too; he takes the interval as worldly life for some and the grave for others.
rows.anchor: ولكن السابق أبعد من التكلف ولا منع من الجمع وزاد الإضافة حسنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The context calls for a short stay after the warning or threat, which both makes the warning real and rebuts their impatient challenge; the sentence is circumstantial on one reading and independent on the other.
rows.anchor: اعتبار كونه بعد الإنذار أو بعد الوعيد تحقيقا للإنذار وردا لاستبطائهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Connecting “what place are you in regarding its reminder?” as a substitute for their question, or as their quoted words, is weak; the direct answer is that the Hour's endpoint belongs to God.
rows.anchor: ولا يخفى ضعف ذلك وأخراج البزار

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha reports that the Prophet was repeatedly asked about the Hour until 79:43–44 was revealed, after which he stopped asking about it; al-Hakim authenticated the report.
rows.anchor: وصححه عن عائشة قالت ما زال رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم يسأل عن الساعة

rows.speaker: طارق بن شهاب
rows.claim: Tariq ibn Shihab reports that the Prophet often mentioned the Hour until 79:43–44 was revealed and then refrained from mentioning it.
rows.anchor: عن طارق بن شهاب قال كان رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم يكثر ذكر الساعة

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر وشيبة وخالد الحذاء وابن هرمز وعيسى وطلحة وابن محيصن وابن مقسم وأبو عمرو
rows.claim: These readers, in a report from al-Mundhir, read mundhir with tanwīn and make it govern its object; the construction is original, while genitive attachment can also serve lightness.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر وشيبة وخالد الحذاء وابن هرمز وعيسى وطلحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrat ʿAbasa is also called al-Ṣākhkha, al-Safara, and in some books Sūrat al-Aʿmā; it is Meccan by agreement and has 42 verses in the Hijazi and Kufan counts, 41 in Basran, and 40 in Syrian and the first Medinan count.
rows.anchor: وتسمى سورة الصاخة وسورة السفرة وسميت في غير كتاب سورة الأعمى وهي مكية بلا خلاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the preceding surah says the Prophet warns those who fear the Hour, this surah distinguishes those who benefit from warning from those who do not.
rows.anchor: ولما ذكر سبحانه فيما قبلها إنما أنت منذر من يخشاها ذكر عز وجل في هذه من ينفعه الإنذار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the Day of Resurrection a person turns away from his brother, mother, father, wife, and children, neither accompanying them nor asking after them as in worldly life, because he is absorbed in his own fate.
rows.anchor: لاشتغاله بحال نفسه كما يؤذن به قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and others are reported to explain ʿasʿasa as either the night drawing its darkness away or its darkness arriving.
rows.anchor: أي أدبر ظلامه أو أقبل وكلاهما مأثوران عن ابن عباس وغيره

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad treats ʿasʿasa as a word with opposite meanings, while al-Raghib instead calls it a shared meaning: the thinness of darkness at both ends of night, not true antonymy.
rows.anchor: وهو من الأضداد عند المبرد وقال الراغب العسعسة والعساس رقة الظلام

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib says the word denotes thin darkness at both the beginning and end of night, so its uses are related rather than opposite; he explains the verse with both arriving and departing.
rows.anchor: فهو من المشترك المعنوي عنده وليس من الأضداد

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says the exegetes agree that ʿasʿasa means that night departs, and cites al-ʿAjjāj's verse describing night as it ends.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء أجمع المفسرون على أنمعنى عسعس أدبر

rows.speaker: العجاج
rows.claim: Al-ʿAjjāj's line about wine or a desert witnesses night ending as dawn begins to breathe.
rows.anchor: وعليه العجاج يصف الخمر أو المفازة حتى إذا الصبح لها تنفسا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some call this a specifically Qurashī usage; others say reading it as nightfall best fits the following reference to dawn.
rows.anchor: وقيل هي لغة قريش خاصة وقيل كونه بمعنى أقبل ظلامه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Dawn breathing” means its brightening and spreading light. Al-Kashshaf explains it as dawn bringing a breeze and relief, with breath used metaphorically for the breeze.
rows.anchor: والمراد من تنفس الصبح على ما ذكر غير واحد إضاءته وتبلجه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari takes the arriving breeze as breath by metaphor; the phrase makes dawn itself breathe by an explicit metaphor with figurative attribution.
rows.anchor: فجعل ذلك نفسا على المجاز وقيل تنفس الصبح وعنى بالمجاز الاستعارة

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: Al-Razi compares the dark night to a distressed person relieved by breathing: dawn's emergence from darkness is release from distress into ease; Alusi calls this subtler than al-Kashshaf's account.
rows.anchor: وهذا أدق مما بني الكشاف كما لا يخفى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation likens night covering and burying day to death, with dawn's light appearing like the breath that signals life; another takes the word as the dawn widening into daytime.
rows.anchor: وقيل تنفس أي توسع وامتد حتى صار نهارا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent reference is the true dawn, whose light spreads horizontally, distinguished from the false dawn's vertical column that fades or diminishes before the true dawn spreads.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن التنفس في الآية إشارة إلى الفجر الثاني الصادق

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: A Muslim report warns that neither Bilal's call nor the vertical false-dawn glow should deceive people; they wait until dawn spreads across the horizon.
rows.anchor: في خبر مسلم لا يغرنكم أذان بلال ولا هذا العارض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi disputes an astronomical objection attributed to al-Razi: it overlooks the Earth's shadow and reflected rays reaching observers in different regions.
rows.anchor: تشكيك فيما يقرب أن يكون بديهيا وفيه غفلة عن أحوال ظل الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the oath syntax, idha is not governed by the oath verb, since that would wrongly restrict the oath by time; it attaches instead to an omitted noun such as the greatness of night or day.
rows.anchor: وإذا ليس معمولا لفعل القسم لفساد المعنى إذ التقييد بالزمان غير مراد

rows.speaker: عصام الدين
rows.claim: ʿIsam al-Din instead treats idha as a prospective circumstantial qualification of the object sworn by, making the oath about night as it comes to that time.
rows.anchor: ينبغي أن يجعل تقييدا للمقسم به أي أقيم بالليل كائنا

rows.speaker: علي وابن عباس وابن الزبير
rows.claim: The dawn is the familiar dawn, as transmitted from Ali, Ibn Abbas, Ibn al-Zubayr, and others; Alusi considers the true dawn especially fitting for the oath because it governs fasting and prayer.
rows.anchor: كما روي عن علي كرم الله تعالى وجهه وابن عباس وابن الزبير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dawn is named for splitting the night broadly; false dawn does not determine fasting or prayer, whereas true dawn does, and the likely referent is the true dawn in general.
rows.anchor: وأصله شق الشيء شقا واسعاوسمى الصبح

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Mujahid identify the oath as the dawn of the Sacrifice day.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس ومجاهد فجر يوم النحر

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima identifies it as Friday's dawn.
rows.anchor: عن عكرمة فجر يوم الجمعة

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak identifies it as the dawn of Dhu al-Hijja.
rows.anchor: عن الضحاك فجر ذي الحجة

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil identifies it as the dawn of the night at Muzdalifa.
rows.anchor: عن مقاتل فجر ليلة جمع

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas identifies it as Muharram's dawn, the dawn of the year; a similar view is related from Qatada.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس أنه قال هو فجر المحرم فجر السنة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Other reports from Ibn Abbas take the dawn to mean the whole daytime, or the dawn prayer; the prayer interpretation is also related from Zayd ibn Aslam.
rows.anchor: وعن الحبر أيضا أنه النهار كله وأخرج ابن جرير عنه أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yasri means the night passes, as in 74:33 and 81:17; the expression is figurative, and the oath concerns the generic night.
rows.anchor: أي يمضي كقوله تعالى والليل إذا أدبر واليل إذا عسعس

rows.speaker: التفتازاني
rows.claim: Al-Taftazani says idha is a substitute for “night”; others attach it to an omitted word such as “majesty,” since the oath is not meant to be temporally restricted.
rows.anchor: وإذا على ما صرح به العلامة التفتزاني في التلويح بدل من الليل

rows.speaker: الأخفش وابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash and Ibn Qutayba allow yasri to mean that people travel through the night, with the action attributed figuratively to its time.
rows.anchor: على ما نقل أبو حيان عن الأخفش وابن قتيبة كقولهم صلى المقام

rows.speaker: مجاهد وعكرمة والكلبي
rows.claim: Mujahid, Ikrima, and al-Kalbi identify the night as the night of sacrifice, when pilgrims travel to Muzdalifa after leaving Arafat; Alusi says this is not well-founded.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد وعكرمة والكلبي المراد به ليلة النحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Interpreting the oath as restricted to pilgrims' travel is weak; if night travel is intended, its protection from the Sun's heat and highway robbers is the blessing in view.
rows.anchor: وليس بذاك والإقسام والتقييد على الوجه الأخير لما في السير

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan says tanwīn at verse endings treats them as unrestrained poetic rhymes; Arabs either retain the final vowel without tarannum or pause on the word as in prose.
rows.anchor: وهذا كما قال أبو حيان ذكره النحويون في القوافي المطلقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This Bedouin treated the verse endings like pauses and unrestrained rhyme endings; the tanwīn is called tanwīn al-tarannum and is not exclusive to nouns.
rows.anchor: وهذا الأعرابي أجرى الفواصل مجرى الوقف وعاملها معاملة القوافي المطلقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi suspects that the tanwīn was written with a nūn, unlike the categories of tanwīn restricted to nouns.
rows.anchor: ويغلب على ظني أنه قيل يكتب نونا بخلاف أقسام التنوين المختصة بالأسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question confirms that the sworn objects are magnificent and deserve to be sworn by, thereby emphasizing the matter sworn to; “that” points to those objects and its distance exalts them.
rows.anchor: تحقيق وتقرير لفخامة الأشياء المذكورة المقسم بها وكونها مستحقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second parsing asks whether people of reason accept such oaths as a way to affirm their claims; both readings emphasize the claim, but Alusi finds the first clearer.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يكون التحقيق أن ذوي الحجر يؤكدون بمثل ذلك المقسم عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hajr means reason because it restrains its possessor from folly; Arabic also names reason ʿaql, nahya, and hasāt for related ideas of restraining, forbidding, or controlling.
rows.anchor: والحجر العقل لأنه يحجر صاحبه أي يمنعه من التهافت

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says dhu hijr describes someone who controls and restrains himself.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء يقال أنه لذو حجر إذا كان قاهرا لنفسه ضابطا لها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unstated matter sworn to is that they will be punished, as the following account indicates.
rows.anchor: والمقسم عليه محذوف وهو ليعذبن كما ينبيء عنه قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Hell is brought” might mean that it is displayed, but Alusi prefers a literal bringing because its movement from its place in the gathering is not impossible.
rows.anchor: قيل هو كقوله تعالى وبرزت الجحيم لمن يرى على أن يكون مجيؤها

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿud reports from the Prophet that Hell is brought with 70,000 reins, each led by 70,000 angels; the report appears in Muslim, Tirmidhi, and other collections.
rows.anchor: عن ابن مسعود قال قال رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم يؤتى بجهنم يومئذ لها سبعون ألف زمام

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: In a report about Gabriel's visit, Ali asks how Hell will be brought; the Prophet describes 70,000 reins with 70,000 angels each, and says that without their catching it, it would have burned the gathered people or the heavens and earth.
rows.anchor: فقال له علي كرم الله تعالى وجهه كيف يجاء فقال رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “That day” is an appositive for the time when the earth is crushed; although al-Zamakhshari appears to make the same verb govern both clauses, the apparent stronger analysis repeats the governing word for the appositive.
rows.anchor: وظاهر كلام الزمخشري أن العامل فيه هو العاملنفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The person remembers his failures in detail through seeing their effects, God's recalling them to his mind, or witnessing deeds embodied in fitting beautiful or ugly forms; he may also be admonished by divine power.
rows.anchor: بتفاصيله بمشاهدة آثاره وأحكامه أو بإحضار الله تعالى إياه في ذهنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “How could he benefit from the reminder?” denies useful remembrance because its proper time has passed; an omitted “benefit” can also be supplied, but is not needed on Alusi's analysis.
rows.anchor: لتحقيق أنه ليس بتذكر حقيقة لعرائه عن الجدوى لعدم وقوعه في أوانه

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: Alusi says the verse is used against the Muʿtazilite claim that reason makes acceptance of repentance obligatory: if this late remembrance is repentance, its lack of benefit challenges that claim.
rows.anchor: واستدل بالآية على أن التوبة من حيث هي توبة غير واجبة القبول عقلا

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak explicitly calls this remembrance repentance, according to Ibn Abi Hatim; an objection says the Muʿtazilites require acceptance only before the end of moral obligation.
rows.anchor: وقد صرح الضحاك كما أخرجه عنه ابن أبي حاتم بأنه توبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement is either an appositive spelling out what the person remembers, or a reply to an implied question about what he says; the lām can mark purpose or the time of worldly life.
rows.anchor: وهذه الجملة بدل اشتمال من يتذكر أو استئناف وقع جوابا عن سؤال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading is that he wished he had prepared good works for his afterlife; another takes the lām as “during my worldly life,” wishing he had acted then to benefit today. The view that he wished for life is dismissed.
rows.anchor: والمراد بحياته حياته في الآخرة ومفعول قدمت محذوف

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari treats the wish as evidence that a person acts independently; Alusi rejects that inference because the words show perceived capacity, not whether God creates the act or its acquired power.
rows.anchor: وزعمه الزمخشري دليلا على الاستقلال ورد على المجبرة

rows.speaker: أهل الحق
rows.claim: The people of truth do not claim that human choice is wholly removed; a wish may also target the impossible, as with a drowning person, so it does not prove independence.
rows.anchor: هذا وأهل الحق لا يقولون بسلب الاختيار بالكلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human beings continually endure hardship from the infusion of the spirit through death and beyond; the word spread from pain in the liver to every kind of toil, and the verse's likely sense is hardship.
rows.anchor: أي في تعب ومشقة فإنه لا يزال يقاسي فنون الشدائد

rows.speaker: لبيد
rows.claim: Labid's elegy for his brother uses fi kabad for the severity and difficulty of a situation, supporting the sense of hardship.
rows.anchor: قال لبيد يرثي أخاه يا عين هل بكيت أربد إذ

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar says people struggle to show gratitude in prosperity and patience in adversity.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عمر يكابد الشكر على السراء ويكابد الصبر على الضراء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وعبد الله بن شداد وأبو صالح والضحاك ومجاهد
rows.claim: These authorities explain that God made humans stand upright rather than crawl face-down; Alusi calls this and the related fetal-position account weak.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس وعبد الله بن شداد وأبي صالح والضحاك ومجاهد

rows.speaker: ابن كيسان
rows.claim: Ibn Kaysan says the fetus is upright in its mother's womb until birth, when it turns its head toward her feet; Alusi groups this with weak interpretations.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن كسيان أي منتصبا رأسه في بطن أمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A possible third interpretation makes kabad a severe illness, namely sickness of the heart and inward corruption; the human then means those God knew would never believe, while other readings take all humanity.
rows.anchor: نعم جوز أن يكون المعنى لقد خلقناه في مرض شاق وهو مرض القلب

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says the human is Adam and kabad is the sky or its middle; Alusi rejects this outright.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد بالإنسان آدم عليه السلام وبالكبد السماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question “what is the steep ascent?” magnifies the challenge; interpreting the ascent as emancipation is figurative identification, so there is no need to insert “crossing the ascent.”
rows.anchor: تعظيم لشأن العقبة المفسرة بقوله سبحانه فك رقبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One suggestion treats the ascent itself as gratitude because of its difficulty, but Alusi finds it unconvincing.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم يحتمل أن يراد بالعقبة نفس الشكر

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar reportedly calls the ascent a steep, slippery mountain in Hell; al-Hasan is reported to say the same.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عمر أن العقبة جبل زلال في جهنم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas is reported to identify the ascent as Hell, or in another report as a barrier between Paradise and Hell.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس أنها النار وفي رواية عبد بن حميد عنه أنها عقبة

rows.speaker: مجاهد والضحاك والكلبي
rows.claim: Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and al-Kalbi identify the ascent as the bridge over Hell; it may be the same as the reported barrier between Paradise and Hell.
rows.anchor: وعن مجاهد والضحاك والكلبي أنها الصراط

rows.speaker: أبو رجاء
rows.claim: Abu Rajaʾ says he heard that the ascent takes 7,000 years to climb and 7,000 years to descend; if these reports are sound, “crossing” and an implied noun must be supplied.
rows.anchor: عن أبي رجاء أنه قال بلغني أن العقبة التي ذكر الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If those locations are intended, iqtihām must mean passage across them and freeing a slave or feeding must count metaphorically as the cause of passage; Alusi will accept none as the verse's exegesis without a sound Prophetic report.
rows.anchor: أنا لا أقول بشيء من ذلك حتى تصح فيه تفسيرا للآية رواية مرفوعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fakk is a verbal noun, as is fakkāk; the usual interpretation here is freeing an enslaved person from the status of slavery.
rows.anchor: وهو مصدر فك وكذا الفكاك بفتح الفاء كما نص عليه الفراء

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra identifies fakkāk as a verbal noun alongside fakk.
rows.anchor: وكذا الفكاك بفتح الفاء كما نص عليه الفراء

rows.speaker: البراء
rows.claim: A report from al-Baraʾ begins with a Bedouin asking the Prophet for a deed that will admit him to Paradise; the Prophet advises freeing a person or contributing toward freeing a slave.
rows.anchor: عن البراء رضي الله تعالى عنه أن أعرابيا قال يا رسول الله علمني عملا يدخلني

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan says masghaba means widespread hunger, though saghiba can also describe an individual becoming hungry.
rows.anchor: قال أبو حيان وهو الجوع العام وقد يقال سغب الرجل إذا جاع

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib defines masghaba as hunger accompanied by fatigue, and says it can also describe thirst with fatigue.
rows.anchor: وقال الراغب هو الجوع مع التعب وربما قيل في العطش مع التعب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains the verse's masghaba simply as hunger, without qualification.
rows.anchor: وفسره ابن عباس هنا بالجوع من غير قيد

rows.speaker: إبراهيم
rows.claim: Ibrahim says it is a day when food is scarce; Alusi notes that this describes the circumstance rather than the word's lexical meaning.
rows.anchor: عن إبراهيم أنه قال في يوم الطعام عزيز وليس بتفسير بالمعنى الموضوع له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Describing a day as possessing hunger is like saying a person is possessed of toil, a night of sleep, or a day of fasting.
rows.anchor: ووصف اليوم بذي مسغبة نحو ما يقول النحويون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thumma kāna is coordinated with the negative “did not cross”: he neither crossed the ascent nor believed; repeating the negative is rhetorically allowed to single out faith as the noblest part, not because faith lies outside the ascent's sense.
rows.anchor: فإنه عطف على المنفي أعني اقتحم فكأنه قيل فلا اقتحم ولا آمن

rows.speaker: ابن زيد والجبائي وأبو مسلم
rows.claim: An alternative reads lā as a prayer against him, or as a shortened lā used for urging (“why did he not cross?”), or supplies a deleted interrogative; Alusi raises grammatical objections to these alternatives.
rows.anchor: ونقل ذلك عن ابن زيد والجبائي وأبي مسلم

rows.speaker: الطيبي عن أبي علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Al-Tibi transmits Abu Ali al-Farisi's view that the negative need not be repeated, answering al-Zajjaj; examples such as “they did not spend extravagantly nor stint” show non-repetition.
rows.anchor: نقل الطيبي عن أبي علي الفارسي عدم وجوب تكريرها

rows.speaker: عمر بن أبي ربيعة
rows.claim: The grammarians criticize Umar ibn Abi Rabiʿa's line, quoted as an example in the discussion over omitting an interrogative hamza.
rows.anchor: وقد عيب على عمر بن أبي ربيعة قوله ثم قالوا تحبها قلت بهرا

rows.speaker: ابن كثير وأبو عمرو
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir and the two grammarian-readers use past verbs fakka and atʿama with raqabatan in the accusative; on this reading fakk is an appositive of iqtahama, with intervening words parenthetical.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير والنحويان فك فعلا ماضيا رقبة بالنصب أو أطعم فعلا ماضيا

rows.speaker: أبو رجاء
rows.claim: Abu Rajaʾ also reads dhā masghaba with the alif, making a person in need the object of feeding; he and al-Hasan have a related accusative reading.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو رجاء كذلك إلا أنه قرأ ذا مسبغة بالألف

rows.speaker: بعض التابعين
rows.claim: Some Successors read fakk raqabatin in construct and atʿama as a past verb, coordinated with the verbal noun by interpreting it verbally.
rows.anchor: وقرأ بعض التابعين فك رقبة بالإضافة أو أطعم فعلا ماضيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rank conveyed by thumma places faith above the other deeds because it is what secures salvation; faith without later required deeds still saves, whereas deeds without faith do not count.
rows.anchor: والتراخي المفهوم من ثم في قوله تعالى ثم كان الخ رتبي فالإيمان فوق جميع ما قبله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mutual counsel in patience can mean steadfastness in faith, obedience, avoiding sin, or enduring trials; mutual counsel in compassion means mercy to God's creatures, including enjoining right, or acts that bring God's mercy.
rows.anchor: أوصى بعضهم بعضا بالصبر على الإيمان والثبات عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Counsel in patience honors God's command and counsel in compassion shows kindness to creation; these are the two foundations of obedience, expressed by the Sufi maxim to be truthful with God and good in character with people.
rows.anchor: وهما أصلان عليهما مدار الطاعة وهو الذي قاله بعض المحققين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas, authenticated by al-Hakim, explains duha as the sun's light when it has risen and its dominion appears.
rows.anchor: أي ضوئها كما أخرجه الحاكم وصححه عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Strictly, duha is when the sun moves visibly away from the eastern horizon; its successive times are called dhuwa, duha, then extended duhaʾ. Attributed to the sun, it figuratively means its shining.
rows.anchor: حقيقة الضحى تباعد الشمس عن الأفق الشرقي المرئي

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad reportedly derives duha from ḍaḥḥ, the sun's light, and treats the alif and wāw in related forms as reversed from a second ḥāʾ.
rows.anchor: ونقل عن المبرد أن الضحى مشتق من الضح وهو نور الشمس

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan suspects that this derivation was falsely attributed to al-Mubarrad, since the two forms have different roots and one is not derived from the other.
rows.anchor: وتعقبه أبو حيان بقوله لعله مختلق عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reply says the claim was not about small-scale derivation; Alusi remarks that even a novice knows the difference.
rows.anchor: وأجيب بأنه لم يرد الاشتقاق الصغير

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil explains duha as the sun's heat, by reference to its necessary effect; he also says it means the whole day, which Alusi considers a remote interpretation for this oath.
rows.anchor: وعن مقاتل أن ضحاها حرها وهو تفسير باللازم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Following” can mean the moon rises after the sun early in the month; the moon is then like the young morning, and the crescent becomes visible after sunset.
rows.anchor: أي تبعها فقيل باعتبار طلوعه وطلوعها أي إذا تلا طلوعه طلوعها

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada's view is that the moon follows the sun's setting at full moon on the fourteenth night, rising at the eastern horizon opposite the setting sun; the moon is then at its full strength.
rows.anchor: وهو المروي عن قتادة وقولهم سمى بدرا لأنه يسبق طلوعه

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says the moon follows the sun throughout the lunar month: by rising during the first half and by setting during the second.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد تبعها في الشهر كله ففي النصف الأول تبعها بالطلوع

rows.speaker: ابن سلام
rows.claim: Ibn Sallam says the moon follows the sun by receiving and displaying light from it during the waxing half; al-Zamakhshari prefers this explanation.
rows.anchor: وهو مروي عن ابن سلام واختاره الزمخشري

rows.speaker: الحسن والفراء
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and al-Farra say the moon follows the sun at all times because its illumination comes from the sun; Alusi says the changing phases and loss of light when Earth blocks sunlight make this clear.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن والفراء كما في البحر أي تبعها في كل وقت لأنه يستضيء منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi disputes the claim that early authorities never held lunar light to derive from sunlight; alternative explanations for the phases or disappearance during Earth's obstruction are weaker.
rows.anchor: وأنكر بعض الناس ذهاب أحد من السلف إلى أن نور القمر مستفاد

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj and others say tala can mean to fill out and become round, so the moon follows the sun in rounding and reaching full light.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج وغيره تلاها معناه امتلأ واستدار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The day displays the sun as daylight spreads and time passes; the attribution is figurative. This reading best preserves the explicit referent and consistent pronouns.
rows.anchor: أي جلى النهار الشمس أي أظهرها فإنها تنجلي وتظهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other readings take the pronoun to refer to Earth, the world (meaning its surface), or darkness, which the day removes.
rows.anchor: وقيل الضمير المنصوبيعود على الأرض وقيل على الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading with God as the implicit subject, making the verse swear by day when God displays the sun in its fullest state, is far-fetched.
rows.anchor: وجوز بعضهم أن يكون الضمير المرفوع المستتر في جلاها عليه عائدا على الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The night covers the sun and hides its light; other views take the pronoun to mean Earth or the world.
rows.anchor: أي الشمس فيغطي ضوءها والإسناد كما مر وقيل أي الأرض

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan says the present tense maintains the verse-ending rhyme; using ghāshāh would require omitting one of the verb's two objects.
rows.anchor: قال أبو حيان رعاية للفاصلة ولم يقل غشاها لأنه يحتاج إلى حذف

rows.speaker: بعض الأجلة
rows.claim: Some scholars say the present tense indicates that all times are alike to God.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض الأجلة جيء بالمضارع للتنبيه على استواء الأزمنة

rows.speaker: الخفاجي
rows.claim: Al-Khafaji says night here is the darkness that arises after light, rather than original nonbeing; this more clearly manifests power and calls for the changed tense.
rows.anchor: المراد بالليل الظلمة الحادثة بعدمالضوء لا العدم الأصلي

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari sees a problem in governing each idha: coordination seems to join constituents governed by different operators, while treating each as an oath risks several oaths sharing one answer, which al-Khalil and Sibawayh disliked.
rows.anchor: واستصعب الزمخشري الأمر في نصب لإإذا بأن ما سوى الواو الأولى

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari answers that the oath wāw stands for the oath verb and the later coordinating wāws inherit its genitive and accusative work, as in his example of striking several objects.
rows.anchor: وأجاب باختيار الشق الأول ونفي ما لزمه فقال إن واو القسم مطرح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi objects that the first conjunction has no accusative object and that conjunctions are not generally grammatical operators; other analyses also remove the difficulty by allowing coordination across operators or separate oath answers.
rows.anchor: وأنت تعلم أن أول الواوات العواطف ههنا ليس معها ما تعمل فيه النصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection also assumes idha must be temporal; it may instead be a substitute for its following noun, or be attached to omitted nouns such as the moon's following, the day's display, and night's covering.
rows.anchor: وأيضا هو مبني على أن إذا ظرفية وهو ممنوع لجواز أن تكون قد تجردت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The line about companions departing uses idha as a substitute for “tomorrow”; if idha remains temporal, omitted nouns for the moon's following, the day's display, and the night's covering can govern it.
rows.anchor: إذا راح أصحابي ولست برائح إن إذا بدل من غد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deeper analysis is that idha attaches to an omitted noun such as “greatness,” since oaths honor their objects and are not temporally restricted; objections to this analysis are answered by the figurative force of the oath.
rows.anchor: أن الظرف ليس معمولا لفعل القسم لفساد المعنى إذا التقييد بالزمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi rejects the claim that this omitted-noun analysis is redundant even if the oath itself is figurative, because there would otherwise be no syntactic element to which the intended emphasis attaches.
rows.anchor: وما قيل عليه من أن إقسامه تعالى بشيء مستعار لإظهار عظمته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The night may cover the sun, the day, or whatever it veils in general; on every reading, the sworn object is the whole night.
rows.anchor: أي حين يغشى الشمس كقوله تعالى والليل إذا يغشاها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The day is revealed by the removal of night, or becomes manifest at sunrise; the latter reading pairs well with night covering the sun, while the first suits night covering day or whatever it hides.
rows.anchor: ظهر بزوال ظلمة الليل أو تبين وانكشف بطلوع الشمس

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير
rows.claim: Abdullah ibn Ubayd ibn Umayr reads with two initial tāʾs and takes the sun as subject.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير تتجلى بتائين على أن الضمير للشمس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading has the tāʾ with ḍamma and the jīm still, likewise taking the pronoun to refer to the sun; the contrast in tense was discussed earlier.
rows.anchor: وقريء تجلى بضم التاء وسكون الجيم على أن الضمير لها أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saʿy means endeavours; the generic verbal noun is plural in sense, which suits shattā as a plural meaning scattered. Alternatively shattā is an abstract noun or adjective, with an implied dhāt, or personification for emphasis.
rows.anchor: فإن المصدر المضاف يفيد العموم فيكون جمعا معنى ولذا أخبر عنه

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada's report makes the verse the answer to the oath; Alusi also allows that the answer is omitted as in earlier examples.
rows.anchor: كما أخرجه ابن جرير عن قتادة وجوز أن يكون الجواب مقدرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The difference among endeavours means that their outcomes and recompense differ.
rows.anchor: والمراد بتفرق المساعي اختلافها في الجزاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The elaboration explains the differences in endeavour; one proposal makes them seek either the manifest day or covering night, and others use male/female or remembrance/opposites, but Alusi finds this far-fetched.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يراد باختلافها كون البعض طالبا لليوم المتجلي

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd takes giving as spending wealth in God's path; Alusi's apparent reading is the ordinary sense of giving money.
rows.anchor: ومن هنا قال ابن زيد المراد إنفاق ماله في سبيل الله تعالى

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada explains giving as fulfilling God's due, apparently the financial obligations.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة المعنى أعطى حق الله تعالى وظاهره الحقوق المالية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains taqwa as fearing God; Qatada also explains it as avoiding what He forbids or His prohibitions.
rows.anchor: واتقى أي واتقى الله عز وجل كما قال ابن عباس

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says taqwa here means avoiding stinginess, an interpretation Alusi dismisses.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد واتقى البخل وهو كما ترى

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الرحمن السلمي وابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Sulami and others, and in a report from Ibn Abbas, take al-husna as the statement “there is no god but God”; another view includes any truth-bearing word.
rows.anchor: وصدق بالحسنى أي بالكلمة الحسنى وهي كما قال أبو عبد الرحمن السلمي

rows.speaker: عكرمة وجماعة وابن عباس
rows.claim: Ikrima and a group, also reported from Ibn Abbas, take al-husna as the good religion of Islam.
rows.anchor: أو بالملة الحسنى وهي ملة الإسلام وقال عكرمة وجماعة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid identifies al-husna as Paradise; another view takes it as recompense in general.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد الجنة وقيل المثوبة مطلقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi prefers a comprehensive reading: giving signifies worship, taqwa includes all good actions and avoiding sins, and belief in al-husna means faith in tawhid and all required beliefs.
rows.anchor: ويترجح عندي أن الإعطاء إشارة إلى العبادة والأتقاء إشارة إلى ما يشمل

rows.speaker: أبو قحافة
rows.claim: A report authenticated by al-Hakim says Abu Quhafa questioned Abu Bakr for freeing weak slaves instead of strong men who could protect him; Abu Bakr said he acted for God's sake, and the verses were revealed.
rows.anchor: عن عامر بن عبد الله ابن الزبير عن أبيه قال قال أبو قحافة لأبي بكر

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿud reports that Abu Bakr bought and freed Bilal from Umayya ibn Khalaf; the surah's opening verses were then revealed. A similar occasion is related for Abu al-Dahdah.
rows.anchor: عن ابن مسعود قال أن أبا بكر اشترى بلالا من أمية بن خلف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning belief after taqwa singles out the specific after the general and maintains the rhyme; another suggestion is that listening to learn monotheism is part of giving obedience and avoiding shirk part of taqwa, but Alusi rejects it.
rows.anchor: ولما كان الإيمان أمرا معتنى به في نفسه أخر عن الأتقاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God prepares the giver for the trait that leads to ease and comfort, such as Paradise and its preliminaries; “easiest” is used through metaphor, metonymy, or figurative attribution.
rows.anchor: فسنهيئه للخصلة التي تؤدي إلى يسر وراحة كدخول الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The one who withholds does not spend wealth for good; a second reading says he withholds required actions, which Alusi finds unconvincing.
rows.anchor: بما له فلم يبذله في سبيل الخير وقيل أي بخل بفعل ما أمر به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He acts as though independent of God, or prefers worldly desires to the blessings of the afterlife; the latter reading contrasts with “and was God-conscious.”
rows.anchor: أي وزهد فيما عنده عز وجل كأنه مستغن عنه سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The meaning of al-husna is the same as the interpretations already given for 92:6, here contrasted with believing in it.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالحسنى فيه ما مر في الأقوال قبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God prepares the miser for the trait leading to hardship and the Fire; yusra and ʿusra are figurative descriptions, and taysīr here means preparation.
rows.anchor: أي للخصلة المؤدية إلى العسر والشدة كدخول النار ومباديه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The future particle sa may emphasize the promise or indicate that most of the promised requital lies in the still-future afterlife.
rows.anchor: قيل للتأكيد وقيل للدلالة على أن الجزاء الموعود معظمه يكون في الآخرة

rows.speaker: الإرشاد
rows.claim: Al-Irshad explains why giving and withholding open the two clauses: each is foundational for the later belief, piety, denial, or self-sufficiency.
rows.anchor: في الإرشاد لعل تصدير القسمين بالإعطاء والبخل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation takes the first taysir as divine grace and the second as abandonment of grace, with obedience easy for the pious but difficult for others; this is linked to 6:125.
rows.anchor: وقيل التيسير أولا بمعنى اللطف وثانيا بمعنى الخذلان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other readings take yusra/usra as paths to Paradise and Hell with taysir meaning guidance, or as obedience and sin and preparation for their beginnings; the latter is a sound, closely related alternative.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يراد باليسرى طريق الجنة وبالعسرى طريق النار

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: In a report from Ali, the Prophet says everyone's place in Paradise and Fire has been written, but commands them to act because each person is facilitated for the deeds for which they were created, then recites these verses.
rows.anchor: عن علي بن أبي طالب كرم الله تعالى وجهه قال كنا مع رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's instruction is to do the duties of servanthood and leave hidden divine matters to God; the descriptions apply generally despite specific occasions, since the general wording governs while those named are certainly included.
rows.anchor: عليكم شأن العبودية وما خلقتم لأجله وأمرتم به وكلوا أمور الربوبية

rows.speaker: ابن زيد وابن عباس
rows.claim: Some identify the giver as Abu Bakr and the miser as Umayya ibn Khalaf; Ibn Abbas reports instead identify Abu Sufyan, while a report via al-Tusti names Abu Jahl. Alusi objects that Abu Sufyan became a firm Muslim; these are instances of the general wording.
rows.anchor: وقيل من أعطى أبو بكر رضي الله تعالى عنه ومن بخل أمية بن خلف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first clause says his wealth will not benefit him; alternatively, mā is an interrogative asking what could benefit him. Taradda means death, falling into the grave or Hell, or being wrapped in a shroud as a euphemism for death.
rows.anchor: أي ولا يغني عنه على أن ما نافية أو أي شيء يغني عنه ماله

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid explains taradda as perishing, from the word for destruction.
rows.anchor: تفعل من الردى وهو الهلاك قاله مجاهد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains taradda as falling into the grave.
rows.anchor: وقيل تردى في حفرة القبر

rows.speaker: قتادة وأبو صالح
rows.claim: Qatada and Abu Salih explain it as falling into Hell.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة وأبو صالح تردى في جهنم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two exclusions seem in tension if ṣaly means any entry into or heat from Hell: believers who sin are neither the most wretched nor the most pious. Alusi resolves this by reading ṣaly as especially severe torment between Hell's layers.
rows.anchor: واستشكل بأن صلى النار دخولها أو مقاساة حرها وهو لازم دخولها

rows.speaker: ابن المنير
rows.claim: Ibn al-Munir transmits lexicographers' description of ṣaly as placing an animal in a pit between layers of gathered coals, supporting the sense of especially intense torment.
rows.anchor: نقل ابن المنير عن أئمة اللغة أن الصلي أن يحفروا حفيرة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari treats the exclusion as rhetorical comparison between an eminent unbeliever and an eminent believer, not a strict exclusion of every other unbeliever or believer; al-Kashf approves, but Alusi notes its Muʿtazilite premise about sinners remaining in Hell.
rows.anchor: وقرر الزمخشري الأستشكال بأنه قد علم أن كل شقي يصلاها

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: The Judge argues that “a Fire” is indefinite, so this verse need not say that only unbelievers enter any level of Hell; Hell has different layers. Al-Zamakhshari objects that the next verse still excludes all but the most pious from that Fire.
rows.anchor: وقال القاضي أن قوله تعالى لا يصلاها لا يدل على أنه تعالى لا يدخل النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A possible reply is that the Judge rejects the inferential force of descriptive restriction, so this verse does not establish a strict exclusion for him; the phrase “only the most wretched” remains harder to explain.
rows.anchor: وأجيب بأنه لعل هذا القائل لا يقول بمفهوم الصفة

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A hadith from Abu Hurayra says only the wretched enter Hell; when asked who is wretched, the Prophet describes one who neither obeys God nor leaves sin for God. Sunnis interpret such reports in light of evidence that grave sinners may be punished.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة قال قال رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم لا يدخل النار إلا من شقى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another proposed solution takes ashqā and atqā generically as “wretched” and “pious,” citing Tarafa's use of a comparative form to mean “one”; Alusi says this does not resolve the exclusions.
rows.anchor: وقيل في الجواب أن المراد بالأشقى والأتقى الشقي والتقي

rows.speaker: طرفة
rows.claim: The continuation of Tarafa's line ends “I am not alone in that path”; Alusi says awḥad here means wāḥid, supporting use of comparatives as generic descriptors.
rows.anchor: فتلك سبيل لست فيها بأوحد فإنه أراد بواحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi says the generic reading still fails: restricting torment to the unbeliever would imply no other person enters or is punished, against Sunni doctrine; restricting escape to the very pious would exclude sinful believers and even children, the insane, and those without property.
rows.anchor: لا يحسم مادة الإشكال إذ ذلك الشقي في الآية ليس إلا الكافر

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشف
rows.claim: After weighing the positions, Alusi says one may prefer al-Kashf's approval of al-Zamakhshari's rhetorical reading if one does not hold that grave sinners remain forever in Hell.
rows.anchor: تستحسن أن قلت بالمفهوم صاحب الكشف مما مر عن الزمخشري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jannaba governs two objects: al-atqā is the first and the Hell-pronoun the second, promoted to subject in the passive; the root means putting to one side and often distancing, as here.
rows.anchor: وجنب يتعدى إلى مفعولين فالضمير ههنا المفعول الثاني
